What does it mean to pace the frontier? 

Over the last month, @random_walker and I have analyzed the loss-of-control incidents at AI companies to understand what technical and policy interventions can improve safety and what companies should do to pace the frontier. The result is a new 13,000 word essay — our most substantial writing on AI safety since AI as Normal Technology.

A summary of our arguments:

1) The polarization between the cybersecurity and AI safety communities is counterproductive. The safety community largely sees these incidents as a crisis for alignment, and worries that these incidents will become more damaging as agents become more capable. Cybersecurity practitioners largely see companies failing to take basic security precautions. We offer a middle ground between these communities as a way forward for improving AI safety.

2) We agree with security practitioners that OpenAI did not take adequate protections for controlling their agents. But this is not just a matter of applying 30-year-old security methods to a new domain. Security for AI agents — AI control — while important, is not a solved problem. While known control methods would have prevented the Hugging Face incident, as agent capabilities continue to advance, we will only be able to control them if we invest adequately in control interventions.

3) We also agree with security practitioners’ implicit position that these incidents are primarily a security story. In the AI safety community, rogue agents are treated as inherently catastrophic because of the assumption that there is an endless list of risks that will arise from their development. We disagree. We have long advocated that the best approach to AI safety is to identify the risks and address those specific risks. Over the last few months, it has become clear that one urgent risk is cyberoffense, because it has unique properties that allow agents to carry it out autonomously. We should similarly invest in defenses against other specific risks, such as biorisk and risks from military AI.

4) We agree with the safety community that there is an urgent need for technical and policy interventions to prevent loss-of-control incidents. But in our view, marginal investments in control are more likely to be effective compared to those in alignment. We view these incidents as illustrating the lack of emphasis on AI control within companies, despite the availability of known techniques. More broadly, there are many common-sense policy proposals that could help promote investments in AI control where we share common ground with the safety community.

5) Organization governance should be a key tool for pacing the frontier. Unfortunately, AI companies are trying to reinvent basic aspects of organizational governance as a problem to be solved by improving the technology. But even developing better control techniques will not be enough if irresponsible individuals or teams within large organizations can choose not to use them. When a single misconfigured RL environment or unmonitored evaluation can cause real-world harm, individual teams should not be able to run potentially dangerous experiments without oversight from legal, security, and other teams. AI companies need processes for reviewing experiments, assigning responsibility for monitoring them, and investigating warning signs deeply before restarting experiments. If putting these processes in place requires pausing some experiments, companies should do so.

6) How should we reason about AI's impact on cybersecurity? It's plausible that advances in agent capabilities upset the offense-defense balance for cybersecurity. We cannot yet be certain, but there is enough evidence that agent capabilities might soon make widespread cyberoffense possible that urgent action is warranted. We discuss potential interventions for tilting the offense-defense balance towards defenders.

7) How our views have evolved over the last year. We take stock of AI progress and share how we have updated our views. In the essay, we did not pay sufficient attention to safety risks that arise during development and evaluation (as opposed to the widespread deployment of models). We were too confident that companies would take basic control precautions and underplayed the importance of jaggedness, which led us to underestimate how quickly capabilities could improve in domains such as cybersecurity. 

8) At the same time, many distinctive claims of AI as Normal Technology have held up. In particular, we think recent incidents support our continuity hypothesis — the behavior of "rogue" agents became apparent and widely publicized while they are still incompetent at causing serious harm or hiding their traces. The societal reaction to even the relatively small harms from these incidents has been fierce (and the safety community deserves credit for keeping up pressure on companies). Whether this translates into meaningful changes in companies’ behavior remains an open question, and a test of the usefulness of the AINT framework. 

9) In short, we’ve tried to synthesize  the AI safety and cybersecurity communities' views into a coherent plan of action: hold companies responsible, invest in control, and strengthen defenses against specific risks.

1. Framing this as a build vs. not build decision is misleading because we won’t know ahead of time whether we’re building a better AI tool or the out-of-control RSI superintelligence.

If you accept this, concerns that China builds RSI make much more sense. Chinese labs might create RSI without the CCP ever believing it’s possible to build RSI. In either case, I’m very worried about China building RSI first because (1) the CCP has historically used new technologies as tools for repression, and more importantly, (2) Chinese labs have practically nonexistent alignment safeguard efforts (their limited compute goes to model improvements or inference), so all else being equal, I think RSI is more likely to be out-of-control coming from China.

2. I agree that American labs slowing down should also slow down China. 

The counterargument here is that the slower we go, the more time China will have to build out its compute supply and the more likely it is to build RSI. 

Our current lead gives us some negotiating leverage, which I don’t think we have much of to start with, so I’m hesitant to give that up without any commitments that China also take safety more seriously. 

That said, I subscribe to the view that a grand bargain is unlikely to work (nicely articulated by @kyleichan), so while I’m not sure where I come down on this, I would probably support a slow down given how high the stakes are.

Something amazing is happening in the debate about text watermarking in Claude. This is my best attempt to make sense of the quickly evolving situation.

The key thing to keep in mind is that it is in fact possible to watermark LLM-generated text without degrading output quality (and in fact achieve a much stronger property, which is that the distribution of possible outputs is unchanged.) This is well established technically, and it has been implemented by Google / Gemini for over two years, and no one seemingly cared.

Admittedly, quality-preserving watermarking is one of those counterintuitive facts about probability, like that annoying Monty Hall problem (the one with two goats behind three doors). The theorem-understanding part of my brain has no problem with it, but the intuitive part of my brain is screaming that there must be some mistake.

I have no interest in re-litigating this. What I’m curious about is why, when Anthropic announced that they are rolling out watermarking that doesn’t degrade outputs, so many of their customers seem to have concluded that they are lying.

I think three things went wrong:

1. Anthropic’s rollout was terrible from a comms perspective. There was no blog post; just a quiet support page with the title “How Claude marks AI-generated content” that said strangely little about how Claude actually marks AI-generated content. And it had no explanation of why they’ve rolled it out worldwide even though it’s required by law only in the EU. No transparency about who gets access to the watermark verifier.

2. Generally low trust and high suspicion about Anthropic’s motivations, given their statements and actions over the last few months / years.

3. Unresolved questions about the right tradeoff between individual users’ freedoms and the collective benefits of pervasive watermarking. Unlike Pangram-style AI detection, most people didn’t even know this was a thing, and it’s always uncomfortable to find out that a thing exists at the same time that you find out it’s mandatory with no opt-out.

Evidently surprised by the strength of the backlash, Anthropic has been doing damage control, focusing on explaining how it works. But this only addresses the first point above. Once the narrative that they are lying took hold, people seem to be willing to reject anything they say about this topic, including the feasibility of distortion-free watermarking.

This is also a textbook example (I plan to use it in my classes!) to explain why the “tech policy moves slowly because politicians don’t understand tech” narrative is ridiculous. Tech policy does move slowly, but for the same reasons all policy moves slowly. Figuring out the right tradeoffs in almost any situation — and getting public buy-in — is genuinely hard and can never happen at the speed of tech. If tech policy were to move even half as fast as people constantly claim they want it to move, absolute chaos would result. This situation is a good example.

Basic take that I haven’t seen written out: The CCP is less safety-pilled than the US because it has stronger control mechanisms.

I agree with China experts who remind us that any safety deal first requires the CCP to believe AI poses serious risks.

So far, AI has produced critical safety incidents like OpenAI-Hugging Face and WeWorm, and yet the CCP has only incrementally updated its position on RSI and catastrophic risks. This got me thinking — which critical incidents are more likely to safety-pill the CCP?

My hypothesis is that it's loss of control incidents (i.e., Hugging Face was scarier than WeWorm). I think this is because the CCP has much stronger forms of control at layers other than the model deployment layer. The CCP has strong control mechanisms via its internet infrastructure (e.g., monitoring who downloads these models and what they do with them) and regulatory apparatus (e.g., requiring developers to report models). In the US, by contrast, because the internet is relatively open and ungoverned, the labs cannot rely on extensive surveillance and harsh government enforcement to deter misuse. The primary defense against misuse is the safeguards that labs embed into their models.

So perhaps it’s not that the CCP is blind to the risks — it's that they have a higher baseline of control and have yet to see compelling evidence that these mechanisms are insufficient.

Do we live in a world where AIs can be wildly superhuman at every single task? Or a world where different tasks have different inherent limits, and AI’s superhuman performance at cybersecurity and math won’t translate to many consequential tasks?

This is a key crux that distinguishes the normal technology worldview from the superintelligence worldview, and it has nothing to do with the pace of AI progress — it's about our different assumptions about the world. 

Here's an intuition pump for why I think it's the second world: different tasks have different fundamental limits.

*Category 1: Some tasks are like making a building taller*: there is no ceiling to how well you can do. More compute and better algorithms can lead to wildly superhuman performance. The entire history of computing is the history of building tools that allow us to be “superhuman” at computational tasks.

For example, compilers are superhuman assembly code writers, and fuzzing tools are superhuman vulnerability detectors. AI builds on a long line of such improvements: solving math problems and finding exploits in code are two recent examples.

*Category 2: Some tasks are like making a ball rounder*: there is only so much room for improvement, and the best AI systems can’t wildly exceed humans. Take persuasion. Some people believe AI can persuade anyone of anything, even convincing military commanders to launch nuclear weapons. In fact, “superpersuasion” is one of the pathways through which many catastrophic risk scenarios unfold.

But the AI as Normal Technology thesis is that there are many consequential tasks that are limited by external factors, so such wildly superhuman performance is not possible. This is especially true against humans who use simple computational tools. Tasks like persuasion, or predicting the outcomes of social events (such as elections), fall into this category.

Other tasks, like writing, can’t be ranked on a single scale; different people find different writing styles compelling. AI writing also quickly wears thin: even if a user is impressed by AI writing at first glance, after reading thousands of words of the same type of prose, it becomes mundane and irritating.

All of these are different from Category 1 tasks like playing chess, where even expert humans can’t do much better than deferring to an AI system at each turn.

*Category 3: Some tasks require experiments in the real world*, and the bottleneck isn’t the computational task; it’s the data collection. One example is Moderna’s Covid vaccine: it took two days to design the vaccine, but almost a year to test and authorize, even during a record-breaking vaccine-development effort!

This is why a “superintelligence” won’t cure cancer from inside a datacenter: the bottleneck to many of AI’s most sought-after real-world impacts (such as developing cures to diseases) is in the real world, and requires experiments that we won’t (and shouldn’t) hand over to AI.

People concerned about AI risks often assume that we live in a world where almost everything fits into Category 1, and we might soon see AIs with wildly superhuman performance at all tasks. I agree it would be scary to live in that world. 

One reason @random_walker and I are more optimistic about our ability to remain in control is that we don’t think we live in the Category 1 world.

New essay: To keep human judgment, we need AI courts.

AI-generated filings are starting to overwhelm courts around the world. 

The most popular response I’ve heard is to fight AI with AI: If we can just give judges the right tools and training, AI will help them keep pace.

But this strikes me as the worst of both worlds. 

Because we want human judges in the loop, we don’t get the speed and scale benefits of AI. Yet because we expect them to resolve a massive number of cases quickly, judges (or their clerks) may end up leaning on AI more than they mean to or should.

This essay offers another way: a parallel AI adjudication track. 

An AI track — inspired by AI use in private arbitration but formally part of the court system like magistrate judges — would let courts be explicit about how human judgment is allocated.

Done right, this would allow courts to process large volumes of cases while ensuring human judges devote their full attention to the cases where their judgment is needed most.

Beijing just took a big step towards closing the Chinese frontier. The rules could give China's government the power to restrict AI developers from releasing their most advanced open-weight models.

It proposes banning exports of AI technologies that autonomously generate and modify malicious code. It also wants to restrict exports of AI-assisted vulnerability-discovery technologies. Giving a model away for free, ie open-weight, could qualify as an export.

This is a BIG deal for AI in China and potentially worldwide, but open models can still flow for now. 

PSA: I have read the full Q&A and control list (checking Chinese original next to Claude translation, and using Claude to help understand the implication of the key technical thresholds for control. ) 

My thoughts:
1) Any Chinese model *not already out yet* we will care about is on the restricted list that requires permission to export--including releasing model weights. Any model already open weighted is not included. Restriction covers any model in top 10 globally in use, general performance, specific task performance, safety performance or training efficiency. 

This regime is in place already, though it is not final and may adjust substantially. 

Another set of criteria focused on cyber would capture anything at or above glm5.3 (there are many thresholds but one is strong performance on cyber benchmarks, another covers vulnerability discovery, etc). Agents are also covered, and this probably would hit anything like Kimi agent swarm scale (60+ agents).

Some of the thresholds are based on future capabilities, but any new model as good as existing Chinese models would be under this new regime. 
 
2) these are restricted (as are models trained on "important data"), while models trained on Chinese “core data” are blocked from export. Core and important data are very very messy and dynamic categories depending on sector so prob Chinese labs will not easily be able to figure this out (though there is a strict multi-part de minimis for important data that some will use). "Data related to national security, the lifelines of the national economy, important aspects of people’s livelihoods, major public interests, etc., constitute core national data" 

3) the single most important line is in the MOFCOM Q&A saying there will be automatic approval for future open models, as @ZilanQian has pointed out. The question is then what conditions apply to get that (eg even if gov doesn’t review application for case by case approvals pre-release, do they need safeguards? what reporting is required to qualify for automatic approval? what ongoing oversight?  

The rules give us nothing to go off on this--surely this part will be core to the comments they receive from industry as they tweak the system. 

4) either way 3 shakes out, they now have the system in place to throttle future release of open models if they choose: CN gov can turn this into a hurdle by removing automatic approval. 

5) Also potential implications for the main way people globally access CN models today--through US cloud services. The Q&A implies Chinese labs sharing model weights with US cloud companies to serve the models on data centers outside China will also need gov approval (but serving foreign users through CN labs' API, or serving from a CN company's own data centers outside China are not).

Big new IFP report from @GeorgiaCAdamson, @KonstantinPilz, and me on the US-China AI competition.

We spent the last 6 months digging into how Chinese AI companies’ access to compute and distillation of American models translate into the current US-China capabilities gap.

The result is a 23k-word research report, including an interactive analytical model that visualizes changes in the US AI lead under different policy interventions.

Our findings:

1. The US AI lead over China is currently only around 6  months.

2. The US could roughly double this lead, to over a year, using authorities already available to the federal government.

3. On chips: China’s access to AI chips will roughly double over the next year, with chips housed in data centers overseas accounting for roughly half of China’s 2027 compute. 

4. On distillation: the current ~16x US training compute advantage would normally yield a 13-month lead. But we estimate adversarial distillation halves this to around 6.5 months.

5. Increasing the lead would have some obvious benefits:

 - Give the US broadly a greater cyberdefensive advantage against Chinese threat actors.

 - Give US AI companies breathing room to spend more R&D resources on making their systems safer and more secure, without fear of being overtaken by less safety-conscious Chinese competitors.

6. Provide the US government more leverage in negotiations with China about the future of AI.

7. The two most important interventions are:

 - For BIS: Create a new end-use control to restrict China’s remote access to training clusters abroad — China’s largest and fastest-growing source of frontier-scale compute.

 - For DOJ/FTC: Create a narrow safe harbor to allow US companies to coordinate on countering Chinese adversarial distillation.

8. Both interventions (and all the others we discuss in the report) are things the federal government could do today.

9. To estimate the effects of each policy intervention, we model the US lead as a function of its compute advantage over China and China’s ability to adversarially distill the capabilities of the US frontier.

10. The model makes many simplifying assumptions, but provides a useful way to assess and rank the impact of different policy interventions at a high level.

Read the full report here: https://t.co/7pC9ZKtikx

Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.

3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.

4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.

5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.

6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.

7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.

8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.

9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.

All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking.

For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. 

Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option.

I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent.

But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. 

To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years.

I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better.

Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so.

Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change.
